title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, loving, and occasionally argumentative examination of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel about money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and what people will do to get it.
It is also about the Thames, about dust heaps, about the strange persistence of the dead — and about human beings trying to live with some dignity inside a social machine that grinds without mercy.
To unpack all of that, I have three exceptional companions with me today.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished literary critics of his generation.
Sir Edmund reads novels as moral dramas — stories about individual character under pressure — and he brings to that reading a lifetime of scholarship and a beautifully sceptical eye.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, a writer, and the voice behind more classic novel recordings than perhaps anyone alive.
Oliver comes to every novel as a performer first — he hears things on the page that most readers simply miss, and he reads a passage aloud the way a great conductor hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong reader of Victorian fiction who first encountered this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
Caroline pays attention to what it feels like to read — the sentences that stop you cold, the characters who stay with you, the music of the prose.
We begin where the novel itself insists we must — with the great social machine: money, dust, and the extraordinary spectacle of human beings in pursuit of both.
What strikes one immediately about this novel — and what one never quite recovers from — is the sheer comprehensiveness of its satirical vision.
Dickens is not content to satirise the wealthy or the corrupt in isolation.
He insists on showing us the whole ecosystem — every human variety that money, and the hope of money, calls into being.
There is a passage — assigned to me with I think considerable mischief — in which the Secretary catalogues the beggars who write to Mr Boffin after his inheritance becomes known.
And Dickens anatomises them with a taxonomist's precision and a comedian's relish.
The detail that arrests me — and I confess I laughed aloud when I first read it — is his description of their enclosures.
He writes:
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf.
The simile is grotesque, precise, and utterly devastating — and it does in seven words what a lesser writer would need a paragraph to achieve.
Now, one could read this passage as social polemic — an indictment of poverty and desperation.
I think that reading is, frankly, too earnest.
This is Dickens delighting in human variety — in the extraordinary ingenuity with which people construct their fictions of entitlement.
Sir Edmund, I am completely with you on the comedy — but I think the comedy and the tragedy are inseparable here, and that's precisely what makes it so extraordinary to read aloud.
Because when you perform that passage — and I have performed it — you feel the double register operating in real time.
The 'beggars of punctual business-habits' who announce they will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday — that is comic writing of the highest order.
The specificity of the time is the joke — the absurd precision of the desperate.
But then you pause, and you think: these are people threatening suicide in their letters.
And the novel holds both things simultaneously — the ridiculous and the truly wretched — without resolving the tension.
That is not something many novelists can do.
What strikes me — reading this passage for perhaps the dozenth time — is the daughters of the general officers.
That devastating parenthesis: 'long accustomed to every luxury of life, except spelling.'
It's almost cruel.
And yet it's also — I think — oddly sympathetic.
These women were never given the education that would have made the appeal dignified.
The comedy exposes the system that produced them, not just the individuals themselves.
And this, I think, is where the dust heaps as a symbol begin to make their full weight felt.
All of this human material — the letters, the scraps, the fictions of entitlement — it is all, in the novel's terms, dust.
Caroline touches on something I think is central to the architecture of the whole novel.
The fortune itself — the Harmon fortune — has been constructed from dust.
And the will that governs its disposal is, in its own way, as satirical a document as any of those begging letters.
There is a second will — discovered by the villainous Wegg — and its terms, as Wegg reads them aloud, are almost a parody of testamentary language.
John Harmon's own words, as ventriloquised by Wegg:

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Quite enough for him.'
The contempt in that phrase is extraordinary — a man disposing of a vast fortune as though distributing leftovers, and doing so with the air of conferring a favour.
The elder Harmon was, by every account in the novel, a thoroughly unpleasant man — and his will is written in his own image.
And Wegg reading that will is one of the great comic performances within the novel — because Wegg is himself a kind of performer.
He reads it with this extraordinary oily satisfaction — 'Exactly so, sir! I see I take you with me!' — building to the revelation as though he were managing an audience.
And the revelation, when it arrives, is a masterpiece of anticlimactic plotting.
The great weapon Wegg thinks he holds — turns out to be far less dangerous than he imagines.
But what I love is that Wegg's theatricality in that scene is itself a form of begging — he's dressing up an act of extortion in the language of benevolent surprise.
He's not so different from the daughters of the general officers, is he?
Oliver, that connection is exactly right — and it points to something the novel does which I find almost uncanny.
Every character in this book, at some level, is performing a version of themselves for an audience of money.
And yet Dickens keeps interrupting this human comedy with these extraordinary passages of pure, almost impersonal description.
There's a passage — one I return to again and again — where the novel simply gives us the train crossing the Thames.
No characters. No plot. Just the thing itself.

"the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
That last image — 'gone again as if it had exploded' — I find it almost frightening.
It is as if the novel is reminding us, beneath all the social comedy, that there are forces moving through this world that care nothing for any of it.
That sense of an indifferent force moving beneath the social surface — the river, the dust, the machinery of the age — will be with us throughout today's conversation.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at the river itself — and at the extraordinary figures who make their living from it.

segments.title: Bella's Golden Fetters: Wealth and Moral Awakening

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's great last completed novel apart, passage by passage, and hold it up to the light.
Today's segment is called Bella's Golden Fetters — wealth and moral awakening — and it sits at the absolute heart of what this novel is about.
With me are Sir Edmund Leigh, the Oxford critic and moralist who reads Dickens as a novelist of individual conscience rather than social programme.
Oliver Trevelyan, actor and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than almost anyone alive — and who hears the rhythms of this prose the way a conductor hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader, who cares most about the experience of sitting with the text and asking what it actually does to you.
Edmund, let's begin with the Boffins — that impossibly good-hearted couple who inherit the Harmon fortune and find themselves hopelessly, gloriously unfit for fashionable life.
The Boffins present Dickens at his most morally precise, and I think that precision is often misread as sentimentality.
Consider the passage where Boffin addresses his wife — there is no grand gesture, no eloquence, only simple and absolute loyalty.
He says — and this deserves to be savoured —
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
Dickens then delivers the sting with perfect economy: it was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations, and they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
Note the capital U on Unfashionable — Dickens's quiet mockery of a world that would regard this happiness as failure.
What Dickens is saying, I believe, is that goodness is its own sufficiency — and that no fortune can improve upon it.
Edmund is right about the capital U, and I want to linger there a moment, because that single typographical flourish is pure Dickensian theatre.
When you read it aloud — and I have read it aloud rather a lot — you find yourself lowering your voice on 'Unfashionable' as though confiding a great social catastrophe.
And then the joke blooms — because of course the catastrophe is no catastrophe at all.
Dickens trusts the reader to hold both feelings at once: the satire of fashion, and the genuine warmth of two people who are simply happy.
That double register is what the best comic writing does, and Dickens does it in nine words.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is how much Dickens trusts silence — the silence inside the word 'pleasant.'
Boffin doesn't say: 'You are virtuous' or 'You are my dearest treasure.' He says it's pleasant to know her.
That muted word carries everything — contentment, long familiarity, a love that needs no performance.
And it sets a kind of standard — an unmarked standard against which the novel will measure everyone else, including Bella.
Which brings us naturally to Bella herself — and to the question of what it costs to want money, and what it costs to give that wanting up.
Oliver, you've been sitting with John Harmon's great confession — his account of why he came back to England and what he feared.
This is one of the passages I find most extraordinary to read aloud — because it's a man cross-examining himself.
Harmon's speech has that strange, incremental rhythm — each clause adding another layer of doubt, another fear.
Listen to how the repetition works here:
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple beat — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — is prose written for the human voice, not the eye.
Each repetition tightens the coil — you feel the man almost unable to breathe under the weight of what his father's wealth represents.
And what that passage reveals, I think, is something Burke would have recognised: the tyranny of an inheritance poorly conceived.
Harmon's father has not merely left money — he has left a moral condition, a kind of corruption that radiates outward.
The novel makes it very clear, in Harmon's own words, that he knew 'nothing but wretchedness that my father's wealth had ever brought about.'
'Knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my father's wealth had ever brought about.'
This is not a critique of capitalism — it is a critique of a particular man's failure of paternal love.
The money is merely the instrument of a cold and loveless will.
I want to hold onto that phrase 'moral timidity that dates from my childhood' — because I think it's one of the most honest things Dickens ever wrote about a character.
Harmon doesn't present himself as a hero deferred — he presents himself as someone damaged, genuinely unsure of his own motives.
And that's what makes the scheme to prove Bella so charged with psychological complexity rather than mere plotting convenience.
He tells us directly — the thought was to turn the danger he had passed through to 'the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'The thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
The verb 'proving' — assaying, testing — is so cold and so tender at the same time.
So we have a man who disguises himself to test a woman who has herself not yet become the person worth testing for.
Caroline, you've been looking at the passage where Harmon goes over the whole architecture of his deception — asking himself whether it was ever anything but a trap of his own making.
This is the passage that breaks my heart a little, every time.
Because Dickens shows us a man caught in a trap that was entirely assembled from good intentions.
The key sentence is extraordinary for its moral precision:

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
That parenthetical — 'never yet for good within his knowledge then' — is devastating.
It tells us that in Harmon's entire experience of his father's world, wealth had never once acted as a force for good.
That is not satire — that is grief.
Caroline is quite right to insist on the grief — and I think it's important to note that Dickens then confronts Harmon with an absolutely impossible moral dilemma.
The novel puts it with characteristic bluntness: by coming to life and accepting the inheritance he must buy Bella; by coming to life and rejecting it, he must punish her.
'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
The symmetry there — shame against meanness, buying against punishing — is the work of a moralist, not a polemicist.
Dickens is asking what it means to be an honourable man in a world structured entirely around dishonourable incentives.
What I find remarkable from a performer's perspective is the passage about the sailors' disguise — the sheer, almost novelistic daring of the scheme itself.
Harmon and Radfoot in common sailors' clothes, drifting into Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood to observe her — it's the stuff of melodrama, and Dickens knows it.
He gives us the mechanism quite baldly:
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
'Throwing ourselves in her way' — as if they were pieces of driftwood hoping to be noticed.
There's something almost boyish and helpless about it, beneath all the plotting — and Dickens keeps that register beautifully controlled.
Oliver's word 'boyish' opens something important — because the world Harmon is fleeing is, at its root, a damaged childhood.
And Dickens places beside Harmon's story another devastated childhood — the child Lizzie describes to Charley, surrounded by drunkenness from her cradle.
Lizzie's words are very plain and very terrible:
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That qualification — 'if she ever had one' — is Dickens doing something a lesser writer would never risk.
He undercuts the very metaphor he's using — making us feel the absence beneath the absence.
Caroline's juxtaposition is, I think, exactly what Dickens intended — and it resists any simple reading of the novel as merely a story about the corrupting power of money among the wealthy.
Poverty, in this novel, is not romanticised — it destroys with the same thoroughness as wealth, only less decorously.
The father in Lizzie's account is described as 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober' — but, Dickens adds with characteristic care, 'a good workman too.'
That 'but' — 'a good workman too' — is Dickens refusing to traduce even those he is condemning.
It is an act of moral scrupulousness that I find more admirable than almost anything else in his fiction.
Edmund's right — and it's one of those moments where the novel's comedy and its sorrow breathe the same air.
Dickens never simplifies his wretched characters into mere objects of pity — they have their competence, their residual dignity, their 'good workman too.'
And that refusal to simplify is precisely what makes the moral awakening of Bella — when it comes — feel earned rather than arranged.
She is not reformed by a tract — she is reformed by contact with complexity.
Earned rather than arranged — that's a beautiful distinction to leave hanging in the air as we close this segment.

We've heard today how the Boffins model a happiness money cannot improve upon, how Harmon carries a childhood poisoned by wealth into his very capacity for love, and how the novel insists — in passage after passage — that moral transformation is never a simple transaction.
In our next segment, we turn to the Thames and the dust-heaps — to what this novel makes of the matter that surrounds all these lives.

segments.title: The Comedy of Pretence: Masking and Misidentity

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to see what makes it extraordinary.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the novel's most dazzling preoccupations: the comedy — and the danger — of pretence.
Disguise, misidentity, performance, and the masks people wear — for survival, for ambition, for transformation.
With me today are three readers who know this novel intimately, each bringing a very different kind of attention to the page.
Sir Edmund Leigh is the retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that the great novelists live or die by moral imagination — not social thesis.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic audiobooks than any living actor and comes to every novel as a performer first — catching the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments written for the voice.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times — always with strong opinions about who deserves better.
We begin where the novel itself begins its comedy of social pretence — with poor, bewildered Twemlow, and the most inspired piece of furniture-satire in the English language.
The moment Twemlow appears on the page — or rather, the moment he doesn't appear, because he arrives as a piece of furniture — I defy anyone not to laugh out loud.
Dickens introduces him, with absolute deadpan solemnity, as follows:
'There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use.'
'Kept over a livery stable-yard when not in use' — that is the life of the minor aristocratic ornament reduced to its naked truth in half a clause.
And then the dining-table metaphor is extended — with the most extraordinary structural rigour — to describe precisely how the Veneerings use Twemlow to build a dinner party.
They start with him, and then put leaves in him.
The more he is pulled out, the further he finds himself from the centre — nearer to the sideboard or the window-curtains.
The comedy is merciless, but Twemlow himself is entirely innocent — which is what makes it so tender as well as so funny.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the precision of the social observation inside the joke.
Twemlow is not merely being mocked — he is being diagnosed.
His entire social identity rests on a single fact: he is first cousin to Lord Snigsworth.
Dickens puts it with that characteristic precision:
'Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.'
'Its normal state' — as if respectability itself is simply the table before the extensions of vulgarity or ambition have been applied.
And yet Twemlow is the one character in these early chapters who retains something genuine — who isn't entirely hollowed out by the social performance.
One must observe, in Twemlow's defence, that the dining-table metaphor cuts both ways.
Yes, it exposes the Veneerings' social machinery with exquisite cruelty.
But it also quietly establishes that Twemlow is the fixed point — the original measure — against which the pretensions of the nouveaux riches are calibrated.
The Veneerings need him precisely because his family connection to Lord Snigsworth represents something they cannot manufacture.
They can buy new furniture, new plate, new guests — but they cannot buy legitimacy.
And that failure of money to purchase what most matters will echo through every strand of this novel — including, of course, in the figure of old John Harmon himself.
Edmund's absolutely right to bring in old Harmon, because there's a passage about him that reads almost like a footnote to the Twemlow comedy — except it's quietly devastating.
The narrator tells us, with that cool omniscient authority, that despite all Harmon's misanthropy, he recognised that the Boffins were simply unbuyable.
The phrase is this:
'he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt.'
'The powerlessness of all his wealth.' That's not a throwaway line — it's the moral spine of the entire novel.
Harmon's wealth can dress up society, can drag Twemlow out to twenty leaves — but it cannot touch the Boffins.
And the Boffins' goodness becomes itself a kind of performance, doesn't it — at least for a time.
Boffin plays the miser so convincingly that Bella — sharp, perceptive Bella — is entirely taken in.
Which makes the scene of her revelation so extraordinarily moving and so funny at the same time.
She kneels at his side and delivers this extraordinary speech, which I find I have to read in full because no paraphrase does it justice:
'Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
That repeated 'Please' is so exactly right — it's the register of a child asking forgiveness, and yet Bella is anything but a child at this point.
She has earned this recognition through suffering and change.
And the disguise Boffin wore — the performance of greed — was, it turns out, entirely in her service.
The Boffin disguise is the most morally audacious act in the novel — and I think the most underrated.
Here is a man of genuine goodness who voluntarily puts on the mask of a vice he detests — and sustains it, at considerable personal cost, for months.
When Harmon finally speaks of what the Boffins have done for him, the language is almost inadequate to the feeling — and Dickens knows it.
Harmon says, and the parenthesis tells you everything:
'I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin.'
'There are no words to satisfy me.' That parenthesis is Dickens stepping out from behind the character to confess that the English language has reached its limit.
That is not a failure of craft. That is the highest craft.
I want to bring us to a disguise of a very different order — because not all the masks in this novel are worn in the service of goodness.
Bradley Headstone's disguise as a bargeman — worn to commit violence and evade justice — is as theatrically conceived as anything in Dickens.
And the scene where Riderhood reveals that he saw everything — every detail of the transformation — is extraordinary.
He itemises it with this relentless, almost liturgical specificity:
'I see you rise up Bradley Headstone, Master, where you sat down Bargeman.'
That sentence has the rhythm of a verdict. 'You sat down one man. You rose up another.'
And then Riderhood deploys the evidence:
'I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows. I've got them, and I've got you.'
'I've got them, and I've got you.' That's the blackmailer's art in eight words — and it's also, played aloud, absolutely terrifying.
What haunts me about the Riderhood scene is that disguise, which was supposed to protect Headstone, becomes the very thing that destroys him.
He put on the bargeman's clothes to become invisible — to shift guilt onto Riderhood himself.
But the clothes survive him — tangible, incriminating, grotesquely material.
There is something almost classical about that — the disguise as nemesis.
And it stands in the sharpest contrast to Boffin's disguise, which dissolves the moment its purpose is served, leaving nothing but goodwill.
And there is one further layer of disguise in this novel that we cannot quite leave unexamined.
Dickens himself, in a remarkable authorial aside, addresses the reader directly about John Harmon's concealed identity — and defends his own artistic management of it.
He writes, with a confidence that borders on the serene:

'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
The artist's disguise is to make suggestion look like concealment — and concealment look like failure.
It is, if you will permit me the phrase, a confidence trick of the highest order — executed in plain sight.
And that self-awareness is part of what makes this novel so alive on every page.
Dickens is performing, Boffin is performing, Headstone is performing, Harmon is performing — and even Twemlow, poor dear, is performing the role of the respectable dining-table.
The entire society of the novel is one vast theatre — and the question the novel keeps asking is simply: who, if anyone, is watching with clear eyes?
Disguise, then, as both the novel's comedy and its conscience — a theme that touches every corner of this extraordinary book.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has itself been, I think, wonderfully illuminating.
We'll be back shortly to pursue further threads in this inexhaustibly rich novel.

segments.title: Dust to Dust: Boffin's Moral Reckoning

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and with full attention to its extraordinary strangeness.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside the novel's great engine room: dust, money, moral reckoning, and the people it makes and unmakes.
With me are three readers whose company I wouldn't trade for any other.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moral critic of the old school, and a man who believes character is everything and atmosphere is merely the weather.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic novels than any living person should reasonably have read aloud — who hears in Dickens's prose something close to music.
And Caroline Woodcourt — critic and devoted rereader of this novel, who brings to it a reader's fierce loyalty and a fine ear for verbal pleasure.
We begin today with the question of what this novel does with goodness — and with the people who either achieve it, fake it, or destroy it entirely.
One of the things that strikes me freshly each time I return to this novel is how comedy and moral seriousness are never really separated.
Consider Eugene Wrayburn, whom Dickens gives some of the best comic lines in the book — and yet whose moral situation is entirely earnest.
There is a passage where Eugene describes how his father, whom he calls M. R. F. — Most Respected Father — pre-arranged the destinies of all his children before they had the wit to object.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one — three words, and an entire comic theology of parental vanity is demolished.

But notice that Eugene tells us this with what he calls 'every sentiment of affectionate deference.' The mockery is not cruel. It is the defence of a man who has been denied the dignity of choosing his own life.
Edmund is absolutely right about the three words, and I'll confess that when I recorded that passage, I stopped and laughed before I could go on.
The rhythm is everything: 'Was born, and became a pillar of the church' — that gathering of formal dignity — and then the collapse: 'a very shaky one.'
Dickens writes that as an actor writes a pause. The sentence ends, the voice drops, and there it is.

And then the third brother who 'appeared considerably in advance of his engagement to my mother' — which is perhaps the most delicate way in the English language to describe being born out of wedlock.
M. R. F. instantly 'declared him a Circumnavigator' — as if the irregularity of the birth required an especially adventurous destiny to compensate.
What moves me in that passage is the sadness underneath it — barely visible, but there.

Eugene says 'I announced myself and was disposed of with the highly satisfactory results embodied before you' — meaning: here I am, a barrister who does no work and is expected to marry for the family's benefit.
The phrase 'disposed of' is extraordinary. Children disposed of. As if they were objects. As if identity were an administrative problem.
And yet Eugene smiles through all of it — because to feel it fully would be unbearable.
That thinness of the smile over real pain — Dickens gives us that throughout the novel. But he also gives us a very different kind of performance: the performance of charity.
Oliver, you've been thinking about what happens to the Boffins once their fortune becomes known — the extraordinary flood of solicitation that pours in.
It is one of the great satirical passages in the novel, and it deserves to be better known.

The Secretary opens the letters, and Dickens gives us this magnificent inventory: fifty-seven churches to be erected with half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings, seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence.
The accumulation is itself the joke — and it keeps going, until it tips into the sublime.
Then there is the letter from the Duke of Linseed. Dickens sets it up with delicious precision:
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words and a social world entire. The fatness of the letter. The privacy that is not private. The coronet that does all the work the argument cannot do.
And then, marvellously, we learn it was 'lithographed by the hundred' — a personal appeal to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, sent to hundreds of Nicodemus Boffins at once.
The passage is savagely funny, yes. But I'd want to pause on what Dickens is actually doing beneath the comedy.
He is showing us that the entire apparatus of organised benevolence — the charities, the stewardships, the noble patrons — is simply another form of extraction.
Dickens calls it 'dust for ocular use' — dust thrown in the eyes of a man newly made rich, to separate him from his gold dust.
The Duke of Linseed is morally indistinguishable from Silas Wegg. Both are in the business of extracting wealth from Boffin by means of a document and a claim.
That connection is exactly right — and it's one the novel keeps pressing on us.
The Steward's fee is 'limited to three guineas' — that postscript is a masterpiece of what Dickens calls 'thoughtful' generosity.
And the novel doesn't let the charities off lightly either: 'mostly in difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print and paper.'
The money meant for the poor dissolves into stationery. Into the performance of care. That detail lands like a quiet blow.
From the performance of charity to a far darker performance — the performance of power. Edmund, you've been looking at Silas Wegg at his most elaborately villainous.
Wegg is one of those characters who fascinates precisely because he has grandiose moral language for entirely ignoble purposes.
He addresses Mr Venus throughout as his 'comrade, brother, and partner' — a formulation that sounds almost Jacobin in its fraternal excess.
And then there is the scheme itself, which Dickens lays out with a kind of gleeful procedural clarity. Let me read the heart of it:
"He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!'"
And if that were not enough, Boffin is to be kept — and I find this phrase genuinely remarkable —
"in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions."
Abject moral bondage. Wegg does not merely want money. He wants subjugation. He wants Boffin on his knees, morally speaking.
This is what greed looks like when it has had time to philosophise about itself.
Edmund's phrase — 'greed that has had time to philosophise' — is exactly right. And Dickens earns that reading by giving Wegg the full procedural treatment.
There's also something almost comic about Wegg's generosity at the end, where he allows that perhaps 'Halves' is insufficient — perhaps it should be two-thirds, or three-fourths.
'On those points he was ever open to correction.' The man is a masterpiece of self-serving false modesty.
And yet when you play him — and I have, in a radio adaptation — you find he absolutely believes in his own righteousness. That is what makes him terrifying as well as ridiculous.
What I keep returning to is the word 'minion.' Boffin is 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
And then Dickens slips in that revision: 'who now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been previously supposed.'
That careful demotion — from minion to worm — is Wegg granting himself the pleasure of contempt as well as profit.
It reminds me that the novel is very interested in how quickly people who have been powerless reach for cruelty the moment power comes to them.

Cruelty without remorse — and that word 'remorse' takes us somewhere the novel goes with extraordinary psychological precision. Edmund, there is a passage about Bradley Headstone that you wanted to bring in.
This is among the most remarkable pieces of psychological writing in the novel — and I would argue, in Dickens entire.
Headstone has committed his crime, and one might expect remorse to follow. But Dickens refuses that comfort — both to Headstone and to us.
He is cursed with something worse than remorse. Let me read it exactly as it stands:
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
More efficiently. That word is shattering. Not guilt — but a compulsion to perfect the crime, to find what went wrong and correct it, forever.
It is a portrait of a mind in hell that does not know it is in hell — and that, I think, is Dickens at his most morally serious.
When I first read that passage as a teenager, I didn't quite understand it. I thought it was about guilt dressed up in strange language.
But rereading it, what Dickens is describing is something entirely colder. It's the mind as a machine that cannot stop running the same programme.
The detail about the 'defensive declarations of murderers' — how they betray themselves by finding the flaws in their own alibis — that is an almost criminological observation.
And the sentence that ends the passage is severe and exact: this state 'tauntingly visits the offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment every time.'
A sullen unrepentant nature. Headstone is not tragic in the classical sense. He is simply unrelenting — and the universe is equally unrelenting in return.
Edmund and Caroline are both right about the coldness of it, and I want to add just one thing as a performer.
When you read that passage aloud, the rhythm forces you to slow down. The sentence won't let you rush it. 'The slower torture' enacts itself in the prose.

That is a novelist who knows exactly what he is doing on the level of pure sound. The length of those clauses — 'incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently' — that repetition with variation is itself a kind of torture.
Dickens is not describing Headstone's torment. He is making us feel it, sentence by sentence.
And against all that darkness — the extortion, the self-perfecting cruelty, the cold absence of remorse — Dickens places something entirely different. Something almost fairytale-tender.
Edmund, there's a small supper scene — Bella, John Rokesmith, and her father — that you've described as one of the novel's hidden achievements.
I use the word 'hidden' because it is not a famous passage. It does not carry the weight of the great set-pieces. But it does something the novel very much needs to do.
Bella and John Rokesmith, together with R. Wilfer — Bella's utterly gentle father — share a meal in humble surroundings. And Dickens reaches for a nursery-rhyme image to describe it:

"It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!'"
It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.
What earns this moment is the phrase 'by far the most delicious.' Dickens is not being ironic. These people, in these cramped surroundings, are genuinely happier than they have ever been.
And that — to return to where we began — is what this novel ultimately argues is the product of moral reckoning correctly done. Not wealth. Not position. A supper without growling.
I love that Edmund went there — because I think that passage is one of the most quietly radical moments in the novel.
The hobgoblins in the forest are, of course, figures of threat — invasion, discovery, punishment. The fairy tale is full of danger.
And Dickens simply removes all of that. 'Without their thunderous low growlings.' The novel's violence and greed and moral bondage are all absent from this table.
And there are the iron safe's two brass knobs — 'like the eyes of some dull dragon' — watching over them. Still present. But dulled. Tamed.
That image of the money-world reduced to a dull, watchful dragon in the corner — I think that's Dickens at his most tender and most exact.
What I hear in that passage is joy. Real joy, written by someone who knew it was hard-won and didn't want to waste a word of it.
The phrase 'gaily said' — Bella says it gaily. Not ironically. Not with qualification. She is happy, and she says something witty, and it is simply wonderful.
Against Wegg's 'abject moral bondage' and Headstone's slower torture, Dickens places this: a supper that's the best any of them ever had.
That is not a sentimental novelist. That is a novelist who has earned his happiness through sixty pages of darkness.
Earned happiness — through darkness, through dust, through the slow moral education the novel inflicts on nearly everyone it loves.
We've moved today from Eugene's comic inheritance to ducal extraction, from Wegg's baroque extortion to Bradley's cold self-torment — and landed, finally, at a supper table where no one growls.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for this conversation.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment — and more of Our Mutual Friend's inexhaustible strangeness.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been talking about the novel's preoccupation with money, with the river, with the weight of the Harmon inheritance.
Now we want to turn to something equally central: the performance of identity.
In this novel, almost nobody is quite who they appear to be — and Dickens milks that, for comedy, for pathos, and for something genuinely unsettling.
Oliver Trevelyan has been living with this novel as a performer for decades, and I think he's the right person to open this up for us.
The thing about this novel is that it understands performance from the ground up — literally from the river.
Take Gaffer Hexam in one of the early scenes — this is a man performing his own moral authority for his daughter's benefit as much as anything else.
He cuts off the boatman with this magnificent bluntness that is almost theatrical in its economy.
"Let go. Cast off!"
Two sentences. Five words. And an entire character revealed.
Gaffer doesn't argue, doesn't plead — he commands. That's how he defines himself.
And there's something in those sharp nautical imperatives — Dickens chose them because they land like blows.
What strikes me is that Dickens is always watching his characters perform themselves — and he's both amused and a little merciless about it.
The Sloppy passage is the purest example of that in the entire novel, I think.
Here is a young man dressed up to look respectable, and every inch of his body refuses to cooperate.

Dickens describes the tailor's instructions as aiming for "the concealment of the cohering and sustaining buttons" — as if the clothes themselves are a kind of scaffolding trying to hold a performance in place.
"He now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
The body always wins. And there's such warmth in that — Dickens loves Sloppy for being uncontainable.
The word "confessed" at the end of that whole description — "Sloppy stood confessed" — carries so much.
I think Caroline is right to pause on that word — "confessed."
There is an old theological weight to it that Dickens would have felt perfectly well.
What is confessed is the truth beneath the performance — and in this novel the truth is almost always more generous, more alive, than the social costume draped over it.
But I'd resist the reading that sees this purely as social satire.
Sloppy's buttons are not an indictment of class. They are a portrait of a particular soul that cannot be contained by categories.
That is the moral imagination at work — not polemic, but individual truth rendered with precision and love.
And then Dickens gives Sloppy one of the greatest comic reveals in the whole novel — and I say that having performed quite a few of them.
The scene where Sloppy unmasks himself before Silas Wegg — that is pure theatrical craft.
The narrator sets it up with this gorgeous slow-burn entrance — "somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors" — you can almost hear the audience holding its breath.
"Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.
Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's."
The whole torment was a performance — and Sloppy, the boy who can't keep his buttons in, turns out to be the finest actor in the book.
I find that genuinely delightful. And a little moving.
It's worth placing that against the Rokesmith and Bella scene, which is the other great reveal of the novel.
Because there Dickens is doing something almost reckless — he lets the emotion be completely unguarded.
Rokesmith bursts in and there's this extraordinary cascade of adjectives — almost comic in its breathlessness, but also entirely earnest.
"My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!"
And then — and I never stop loving this moment — Bella simply lifts her head and lays it on his breast.
"As if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place" — that parenthetical is doing so much quiet work.
After all the performing and pretending, here is someone finally at rest in who she is.
That is well observed. The novel's deepest argument, I think, is precisely that — that character is not performance but, in the end, destination.
We perform until we discover who we are. And then, if we are fortunate, we stop.
Rokesmith has been performing John Harmon for the length of the book. Sloppy has been performing a dutiful disguise.
Both revelations are moments of, as Oliver would say, the mask coming off — but the moral weight they carry is different in kind.
Bella's acceptance is the graver thing. It is an act of faith in another person's true self — and faith, in Dickens, is never trivial.
Identity as destination — I think that's a wonderful phrase to carry forward.
We've moved from Gaffer's blunt self-assertion on the river, through Sloppy's magnificent and uncontainable buttons, to Bella laying her head down and arriving somewhere true.
In our next segment, we'll be asking how the novel handles the characters who never quite arrive — those whose performances calcify into something darker.

segments.title: Love, Money, and the Architecture of Plot

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're looking today at the architecture of plot in this novel — the machinery of money, inheritance, and disguised identity that drives everything forward.
But what's remarkable is how Dickens keeps embedding human warmth at the very centre of all that machinery.
With us, as ever, are Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt.
Let's begin with Mr Boffin — because the Boffins are really the emotional engine of these early chapters.
What strikes me every time I re-read these passages is how Boffin narrates the past as if it were still present to him.
He's not summarising the history of the Harmon household — he's reliving it, in front of Mortimer Lightwood.
And there's this extraordinary moment where Old Harmon's violence becomes almost farcical — and then suddenly it isn't.
Boffin describes how the old man would, as he puts it,
"catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard."
You start to laugh — that bonnet detail is perfectly chosen — and then comes the sentence that ends it all.
"Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition. The full stop between those two clauses. It's devastating.
I've read that passage aloud more than once, and the thing about "Dropped her" — you can't rush it.
Boffin's voice is doing something extraordinary — it holds the comedy and the grief simultaneously, and neither cancels the other out.
Dickens knew exactly what he was doing with that bonnet — he gives you something to smile at, and then knocks you down.
And the genius is that it's Boffin himself telling the story — a man who witnessed his wife being felled, and yet his account is never self-pitying.
He's simply bearing witness. That's the whole moral texture of the character in miniature.
I think what Caroline and Oliver are identifying is something rather precise — the way in which Boffin's dialect is not a marker of his limitation, but the vehicle of his authority.
He speaks in a manner that polite society would condescend to, and yet it is he who has the full moral picture.
That inversion is characteristic of this novelist at his best.
And the passage that follows — the memory of the seven-year-old boy — is, I would argue, among the most affecting things in the novel.
Boffin sets the scene with that phrase,
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind."
The anaphora — that repeated 'there was' — creates a kind of liturgical gravity entirely at odds with the humble register of the speaker.
Boffin doesn't know he's making rhetoric. And that is precisely why it works.
That passage about the child always makes me stop reading for a moment.
The detail of Mrs Boffin kneeling by the fire, warming her hands and then rubbing the child's cheeks — it's so physical, so tender.
And then Dickens gives us her words — not paraphrased, but directly reported, almost spontaneous:
"I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"
That doubled 'wide' — she can't contain herself even in her own speech.
And then Boffin adds that in years after, on cold nights, she would wake sobbing and cry out: "Don't you see the poor child's face? O shelter the poor child!"
She carried that look for years. That says everything about what the Harmon fortune cost the people who lived nearest it.
And what does Mrs Boffin do when the money finally comes to them?
She doesn't buy a grand house first, or worry about society — she proposes adopting a child and giving him the dead boy's name.
She says it plainly, almost shyly:
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
"Somehow, it would make me easier, I fancy." — that final hesitation.
She's not claiming virtue. She's not seeking credit. She just wants to make restitution to a child who no longer exists.
There is something almost unbearably good about Henrietta Boffin. And the novel earns every bit of it.
I should like to draw the conversation toward the darker architecture of the plot, because the novel sets against this warmth something altogether more sinister.
We have Riderhood's denunciation of Gaffer Hexam — and it is delivered with a kind of reptilian ceremonial precision.
He says, for the record:
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body.
The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
That threefold insistence — 'his hand,' the deed, 'his hand and no other' — is the rhetoric of a man who has rehearsed this moment.
It is false testimony delivered with the cadence of sworn truth. Dickens gives villainy its own eloquence here.
Riderhood is one of those characters who is always performing — even when he thinks no one is watching.
And the cold companion to that, later in the novel, is Bradley Headstone — a man who has stopped performing altogether and simply collapsed inward.
The passage where Dickens describes Bradley sitting by the fire all night — it's unlike anything else in the book.
Dickens writes:
"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard,
its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
Degenerating. Not greying — degenerating. As if the whole biological fact of him is coming apart.
What arrests me in that passage is the phrase 'charmed flame.'
Bradley is not merely being consumed by guilt — he is under a kind of enchantment.
He is riveted to the spot by the very force of the passion that has destroyed him.
This is not a social critique — it is a portrait of a soul in extremis.
One thinks of Macbeth in his long night — a man unable to move, unable to repent, unable to act.
The novel reaches here for something close to tragedy in the classical sense, and I think it earns it.
And yet all of that is being watched by Riderhood, who has no capacity for that kind of suffering at all.
The two of them locked together in that room — the man being consumed from within, and the man watching with cold calculation — it's one of the most claustrophobic pairings in the novel.
And it stands in absolute contrast to what we were talking about earlier — Mrs Boffin warming a child's cheeks by the fire.
The same novel, the same fire, the same night — and the distance between those two scenes is the entire moral range of the book.
That's a beautiful place to pause — the fire as emblem of both shelter and destruction in the same novel.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the novel's river — which plays its own more ambiguous role in all of this.

segments.title: Closing: Redemption and the Refashioned World

utterances.text: We've reached the close of our journey through Our Mutual Friend today — a novel that ends, against all odds, in something very like hope.
But what kind of hope is it, exactly?
A world that contains Riderhood's testimony, Jenny Wren's visions, and Boffin's magnificent contempt for charity patronesses — this is not a simple or sentimental world.
I want to ask each of you: what kind of redemption does this novel actually deliver, and does it earn it?
The question of whether a novelist earns his resolution is, I think, the most important question one can ask of a work of this ambition.
And I confess that what strikes me most forcibly in these closing movements is not the romantic reconciliations — satisfying as those are — but the honesty with which the darker material is handled.
Consider the Riderhood testimony against Gaffer Hexam.
Here is a man of no moral standing whatsoever, reconstructing a confession from a dead man's lips.
The words he quotes are these:
There is no redemption there — none at all.
And yet the novel does not flinch from it.
That moral honesty is, to my mind, the very ground on which any subsequent hope must be built.
Edmund is absolutely right that the darkness earns the light — and I'd go further and say that the novel knows this perfectly well.
But I want to come at it from a different angle, because I think the real redemptive heart of the book is not in its plot mechanics at all.
It is in Jenny Wren.
When she describes the children who came to her in her pain — those celestial figures in white — she does something extraordinary.
She speaks — and I have read this passage aloud many times — in a tone that is utterly unlike anything else in the novel.
The repetition —
It is a chant, a liturgy almost, written for the voice — and it breaks the heart every single time.
I'm glad Oliver went to Jenny Wren, because I think she is the novel's strangest and most surprising gift to its reader.
She is in pain — constant, bodily, exhausting pain — and yet what she gives back is imagination.
The detail that arrests me every time is that line about her birds and flowers.
She says:
That tiny comparative —
And it's not boasting — it's simply true.
Her imagination has been made richer by suffering, not diminished by it.
That, to me, is the redemption this novel actually offers — not rescue from pain, but something made in the midst of it.
Caroline puts it beautifully.
And yet I would add one note of qualification — because I think the novel is simultaneously doing something rather more satirical, and it would be a mistake to let that strand go unremarked.
Think of Mr Boffin's magnificent tirade against the vanity of charity patronage.
He catalogues them with exquisite comic rhythm:
The rhythm of that sentence is almost musical — each title one grade more absurd than the last, the whole edifice collapsing finally into Rokesmith sitting neck-deep in the rubble.
The refashioned world this novel proposes is one where such pretension has been seen through — not abolished, but seen through.
I've performed that Boffin speech, and I can tell you — it's almost impossible to get through the list of Vice-Patronesses without starting to giggle.
Which is precisely the point.
Boffin is a man who has come into enormous wealth and has the extraordinary good fortune of not being improved by it.
He sees the whole machinery of polite philanthropic pretension for what it is — utter nonsense — and he says so, loudly, in his own wonderful idiom.
That, too, is a kind of redemption.
Not a spiritual one — Boffin will leave that to Jenny — but a comic, robust, thoroughly English one.
What I keep returning to is the novel's extraordinary range — the distance between Riderhood's river and Jenny Wren's celestial children, and the fact that both are held in the same book.
Riderhood gives us those words —
— and they land like stones.
And then, in another part of the same story, children in white come down in long bright slanting rows asking
The novel refuses to resolve that tension — and that, I think, is its deepest truth.
A world where foul play and celestial comfort exist in the same breath.
That feels like a fitting note on which to close — not resolution, but honest complexity.
My warmest thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers whose company makes this the finest of novels even finer.
Our Mutual Friend Unpacked will return.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly

Then, the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides
      of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and
      under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over
      the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded
      in the rush of smoke and steam and glare. A little more, and again it
      roared across the river, a great rocket: spurning the watery turnings and
      doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as
      Father Time goes to his. To whom it is no matter what living waters run
      high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their
      little growth of weeds and flowers, turn here, turn there, are noisy or
      still, are troubled or at rest, for their course has one sure termination,
      though their sources and devices are many.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy
      castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint
      James’s, when not in use, to whom the Veneerings were a source of blind
      confusion. The name of this article was Twemlow. Being first cousin to
      Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might
      be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state. Mr and Mrs
      Veneering, for example, arranging a dinner, habitually started with
      Twemlow, and then put leaves in him, or added guests to him. Sometimes,
      the table consisted of Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, of
      Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his
      utmost extent of twenty leaves. Mr and Mrs Veneering on occasions of
      ceremony faced each other in the centre of the board, and thus the
      parallel still held; for, it always happened that the more Twemlow was
      pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to
      the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.

‘John dear,’ said Bella, ‘you’re a good nurse; will you please hold baby?’
      Having deposited the Inexhaustible in his arms with those words, Bella
      looked hard at Mr Boffin, who had moved to a table where he was leaning
      his head upon his hand with his face turned away, and, quietly settling
      herself on her knees at his side, and drawing one arm over his shoulder,
      said: ‘Please I beg your pardon, and I made a small mistake of a word when
      I took leave of you last. Please I think you are better (not worse) than
      Hopkins, better (not worse) than Dancer, better (not worse) than
      Blackberry Jones, better (not worse) than any of them! Please something
      more!’ cried Bella, with an exultant ringing laugh as she struggled with
      him and forced him to turn his delighted face to hers. ‘Please I have
      found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don’t believe you are a
      hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don’t believe you ever for one
      single minute were!’

‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’

      him half a dozen times, ‘and I played it long ago; long afore you tried
      your clumsy hand at it; in days when you hadn’t begun croaking your
      lecters or what not in your school. I know to a figure how you done it.
      Where you stole away, I could steal away arter you, and do it knowinger
      than you. I know how you come away from London in your own clothes, and
      where you changed your clothes, and hid your clothes. I see you with my
      own eyes take your own clothes from their hiding-place among them felled
      trees, and take a dip in the river to account for your dressing yourself,
      to any one as might come by. I see you rise up Bradley Headstone, Master,
      where you sat down Bargeman. I see you pitch your Bargeman’s bundle into
      the river. I hooked your Bargeman’s bundle out of the river. I’ve got your
      Bargeman’s clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained
      green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the
      blows. I’ve got them, and I’ve got you. I don’t care a curse for the
      T’other governor, alive or dead, but I care a many curses for my own self.
      And as you laid your plots agin me and was a sly devil agin me, I’ll be
      paid for it—I’ll be paid for it—I’ll be paid for it—till
      I’ve drained you dry!’

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

      pillar of the church; a very shaky one. My third brother appeared,
      considerably in advance of his engagement to my mother; but M. R. F., not
      at all put out by surprise, instantly declared him a Circumnavigator. Was
      pitch-forked into the Navy, but has not circumnavigated. I announced
      myself and was disposed of with the highly satisfactory results embodied

But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
